Building Betty Wakia's Digital Home: A Blog by Rebbie Afuyaso at Wuhan University of Technology

When Betty Wakia first approached me about creating a personal website where she could share her writing and sell her books, I didn't immediately grasp the weight of what she was asking. She had noticed something in me—perhaps the way I talked about building things, or the quiet confidence I carried when discussing code—and she decided to trust me with something that mattered to her. As a second-year Computer Science and AI student at Wuhan University of Technology, I had built projects before, but this was different. This was someone's livelihood, someone's voice, someone's dream being handed to me with the simple words: "I believe you can do this."

That trust became the foundation of everything that followed. Betty didn't just want a website; she wanted a home for her ideas, a place where her readers could find her and where her books could reach the people who needed them. She explained her vision with the clarity of someone who had thought about it for years—a blogging platform that would also serve as a bookstore, simple enough for her to manage daily but robust enough to grow with her audience. I listened, took notes, and quietly promised myself that I would not let her down.

Project Commence

The early days were humbling. I quickly discovered that building a production-ready site with content management, e-commerce, and a clean reading experience was nothing like the classroom projects I was used to. There were environment configurations that fought back, network issues that tested my patience, and moments when the terminal output felt like a foreign language. But every time I hit a wall, I remembered Betty's confidence in me. She hadn't asked for perfection; she had asked for my best. So I kept going, learning as I built, treating every error message as a lesson rather than a setback.

What kept me grounded was the realization that this project sat at the intersection of everything I was studying. Computer Science gave me the tools, but AI thinking gave me the approach: break the problem down, iterate quickly, test assumptions, and never stop learning. I wasn't just writing code—I was designing a system that had to be reliable, maintainable, and genuinely useful for someone who wasn't a developer. That perspective changed how I worked. I stopped chasing clever solutions and started building things that simply worked, day after day.

There were moments of doubt, of course. When a template refused to load or a dependency clashed with my environment, I questioned whether I was the right person for this. But each small victory—seeing the blog template finally render, watching a test post appear on the page, getting the development server to run without errors—rebuilt my confidence piece by piece. Betty never wavered in her trust, and that steadiness became my own. I learned that doing your best isn't about avoiding mistakes; it's about showing up consistently until the thing works.

Now, as the site takes shape, I find myself thinking about what it represents. It's not just a collection of pages and a payment gateway. It's a statement of belief—Betty's belief in me, and my belief that a second-year student from Wuhan University of Technology can build something real and meaningful. Every line of code, every configuration file, every late-night debugging session has been an investment in that belief. I didn't just build a website; I built proof that trust, when given honestly and received gratefully, can produce something worth sharing with the world.

This blog is the first chapter of that story. Betty Wakia will fill these pages with her words, her research, and her books, and I will quietly maintain the foundation beneath it. I am Rebbie Afuyaso, a Computer Science and AI student at Wuhan University of Technology, and I am proud to say that I did my best for someone who saw something in me before I fully saw it in myself. The site is live, the journey continues, and the trust that started it all remains the most important feature I ever built.
